docs.title: Quantum cohomology of flag varieties
docs.text:
GEOATOMS brings together computed examples and software for genus-zero Gromov–Witten theory. The catalog covers flag varieties and their complete intersections; the Python package gwflags computes their invariants by exact virtual localization.

Explore the catalog Use the software

docs.title: Explore the examples
docs.text:
Browse projective complete intersections, Grassmannians, flag varieties and their sections, or the Fano threefold reference catalog. Each computed entry includes a multiplication matrix and the information needed to interpret it.

The collection includes 131 completed computations. Download matrices and inputs to reuse the symbolic results, bases and gradings in your own calculations.

docs.title: Compute with gwflags
docs.text:
Use the local browser interface, command line or Python API to compute GW invariants and multiplication by the first Chern class. For complete intersections, the returned matrix acts on the flag-ambient sector; Methods and conventions explains its scope.

The stable software is v1.0.5. Download its source ZIP, follow the installation guide, or read the release notes.

docs.title: Software and sources
docs.text:
The open-source gwflags repository contains the localization algorithms, tests and catalog-generation tools. AI coding tools, including Google Antigravity, have assisted software and website development under the contributors’ mathematical supervision.

The threefold classification follows Fanography. The mathematical formulas, conventions and verification procedures are described in Methods and conventions.

docs.title: description: Python API for gwflags: flag varieties, homogeneous bundles, Gromov-Witten invariants, and small quantum multiplication.
GWFlags API Reference
docs.text: gwflags evaluates decorated-tree formulas with exact Python/Sage computations. The default numerical path evaluates the localization sum at two rational torus points; the symbolic path remains available through gw_raw.

docs.title: 1. Root systems (gwflags/rootsystem.py)
docs.text: RootSystemData stores Bourbaki-numbered simple and positive roots, Cartan and reflection matrices, coroots, and fundamental weights. All root and weight arithmetic is exact (fractions.Fraction) and semisimple products such as A2xA2 are supported.

docs.title: 2. Virtual localization (gwflags/localization.py)
docs.text:
GWCalculator implements Graber--Pandharipande genus-zero virtual localization on decorated trees:

  • rfactor(w) evaluates the fixed-point Euler factor;
  • billey(schubert, vertex) evaluates a Schubert restriction by Billey's formula;
  • omega_lie(w, root_idx, d) evaluates the invariant-curve edge factor;
  • kappa_gamma(dt) and i_vertex(dt, v) evaluate tree edge/vertex factors;
  • gw_invariant(coh_classes, beta) sums all valid decorated trees.

The low-level calculator uses an ambient vector indexed by all simple roots. The public FlagVariety methods normalize kept-root coordinates before calling it.

docs.title: 3. Complete-intersection twists (gwflags/cintersection.py)
docs.text:
A homogeneous bundle supplies torus weights and invariant-curve restrictions. For the standard constructors these restrictions come from their supported weight model. Fixed-point weights alone do not determine the splitting of an arbitrary non-split bundle along a curve. The module implements:

  • euler_complete_intersection(gw, K, w) gives the fixed-point Euler class;
  • h_complete_intersection(gw, K, w, root_idx, d) gives the convex edge contribution;
  • gw_complete_intersection(gw, coh_classes, beta, K) performs the twisted localization sum.

Every invariant-curve splitting degree must be nonnegative. This is the curve-wise convexity condition used by the genus-zero twisted theory. For the standard smooth-zero-locus interpretation, assume global generation and a regular section whose zero locus is smooth of the expected codimension.

Bundles can be constructed with O(X, a1, ...), taut_sub(X, node), taut_quot(X, node), dual, osum, tensor, sym, wedge, and quot. The GUI and CLI also accept compact aliases O(a1,...), S(node), and Q(node) with X bound to the current flag. quot(E, F) (also Quot(E, F)) checks that the fiber-weight multiset of F is contained in E with multiplicity before constructing its weight model. This check does not prove that an embedding exists or recover arbitrary extension data; the geometric quotient and its curve restrictions must be justified separately. A legacy split bundle is a list of rows, for example [[1], [2]] for O(1) + O(2) on a one-generator space.

docs.title: FlagVariety(algebra, roots_that_stay, backend=None)
docs.text: roots_that_stay is a distinct list of 1-based simple-root nodes not in the parabolic, in the order used for Picard coordinates. For example, FlagVariety("A4", [2]) is Gr(2,5), and FlagVariety("A2xA2", [1,3]) is P² × P².

docs.title: Curve classes (beta)
docs.text: A curve class is written [ \beta=(b_{i_1},\ldots,b_{i_\rho}), \qquad (i_1,\ldots,i_\rho)=\texttt{roots_that_stay}, ] where the entries are nonnegative integers in the kept simple-coroot basis. The public methods accept this compact vector and embed it at the ambient Bourbaki nodes. A zero-padded ambient vector of length rank is also accepted, but every removed-node entry must be zero. For A3 --keep 2, (1) and (0,1,0) therefore denote the same line class. The returned GW result and progress messages use the canonical ambient vector.

docs.title: gw(coh_classes, beta, K=None, progress=None)
docs.text: Returns the exact genus-zero invariant \(\langle\sigma_{u_1},\ldots,\sigma_{u_n}\rangle_{0,n,\beta}\), optionally Euler-twisted by K. The dimension axiom is checked before localization; a mismatch returns zero. At degree zero this API intentionally returns the classical cup integral when the insertion codimensions sum to the target dimension, even with two insertions. This pairing shortcut is not the definition of an unstable degree-zero GW invariant.

docs.title: expected_degree(beta, n_classes, K=None)
docs.text: Returns the codimension sum required by the dimension axiom after normalizing beta and accounting for the bundle rank.

docs.title: fano_index_and_betas(K=None)
docs.text:
Returns (I_X, betas). With the default ambient curve lattice, I_X is the gcd of the first-Chern coordinates. It is the geometric Fano index when the chosen coordinates give the integral Picard lattice of the zero locus; that identification can fail for low-dimensional sections. A constructor with explicit effective-curve generators instead uses their Chern pairings.

Automatic enumeration uses \(\langle c_1(TX),\beta\rangle\leq\dim X+1\). This gives a finite complete supported list only with strictly positive Chern pairings on all enumerated generators. Mixed zero and positive ambient pairings, or a negative pairing, raise ValueError unless supported effective generators supply a positive bound. Supply small_quantum_multiplication(..., betas=[...]) for a geometrically justified finite list or a deliberately truncated computation. When the entire Chern vector vanishes, multiplication by it is zero, so the method returns index zero and only the zero class.

docs.title: small_quantum_multiplication(K=None, betas=None, progress=None, workers=0)
docs.text: Returns (M, grading, basis_indices) for multiplication by c1(TX) on the flag-ambient Schubert sector. M is symbolic in y<node>, where <node> is the ambient Bourbaki label of a kept root (so kept nodes 1,3 use y1 and y3). betas may be supplied in either accepted beta convention. The matrix uses input columns and output rows. The grading is diagonal with entries codimension − dim(X)/2, and basis_indices indexes X.classes and X.class_words() in their returned order. It is the full small quantum-cohomology operator only when the relevant homology and ambient-completeness hypotheses hold; otherwise it is the flag-ambient block. workers=N distributes independent per-beta blocks over forked processes.

docs.title: Other useful methods
docs.text:
• classes, class_words(), schubert(word), and pt expose the minimal Schubert representatives;
  • gw_raw(...) returns the unspecialized symbolic localization sum;
  • eigenvalues(M, at_one=True) computes the spectrum after setting all Novikov variables to one.

docs.title: 5. Schubert words and interface syntax
docs.text:
FlagVariety.schubert(word) projects an arbitrary Weyl word to its minimal coset representative for low-level exploratory use. The CLI and browser form use the safer published contract: each insertion word must be reduced and minimal for the chosen parabolic. Run info/Space Info, then copy one of the printed words (or use the Add button). Separate insertions with |; pt, id, and e are accepted shortcuts.

For the compact GUI/CLI bundle field, use 3 or 1,1;2,2 for line-bundle rows; Python list notation such as [[3]] belongs to the Python API. In a symbolic matrix, variables are named by ambient nodes, while beta input is in kept-root order unless zero-padded.

docs.title: 6. Minimal reproducible examples
docs.text:
from gwflags import FlagVariety, grassmannian, projective_space
from gwflags.bundles import O, taut_quot, dual, taut_sub, osum, wedge, quot

P2 = projective_space(2)
assert P2.gw([P2.pt, P2.pt], beta=(1,)) == 1
assert P2.gw([P2.pt, P2.pt], beta=(1, 0)) == 1

G = grassmannian(2, 4)
s1, s21, pt = G.schubert((2,)), G.schubert((1, 3, 2)), G.pt
assert G.gw([s1, s21, pt], beta=(1,)) == 1

Q = taut_quot(G, 2)
K = osum(Q, O(G, 1))
M, grading, basis = G.small_quantum_multiplication(K=K)

E = osum(taut_sub(G, 2), Q)
Kq = quot(E, taut_sub(G, 2))
assert Kq.rank == 2

docs.title: How to use gwflags
docs.text: gwflags computes Gromov–Witten invariants and small quantum multiplication for flag varieties G/P and supported complete intersections. The browser interface is the easiest starting point; the Python and CLI interfaces are documented later.

docs.title: Launch the interface
docs.text:
Follow Installation to install the stable software. Then run:

python -m gwflags.gui --no-browser

Open http://127.0.0.1:8642. The server runs on your computer; stop it with Ctrl-C. Use --port 9000 if the default port is occupied.

docs.title: Fastest path: load an example
docs.text:
1. Choose an item from Preset library.
  2. Read the recommended action and expected result shown below the selector.
  3. Click Describe this space, Compute quantum matrix, or Compute one GW invariant as recommended.
  4. Follow progress in the status and log areas. Large index-1 examples can take several minutes.
  5. After a result appears, use Copy input JSON to save the exact form values (including the selected action), or Download result JSON to save the input together with the complete result for later analysis.

The preset fills every dependent field, so an old β or insertion cannot accidentally remain in a new example.

docs.title: The five core inputs
docs.text:
• Lie algebra: A3, B2, C3, D5, G2, or a product such as A3xA3.
  • Kept simple roots: comma-separated Bourbaki node numbers, for example 1 for projective space or 2 for Gr(2,4) in type A3.
  • Bundle K (optional): leave blank for G/P; enter 3 for O(3), or 1,1;2,2 for two line-bundle summands when the variety has two kept roots (use 1;2 on a Picard-rank-one variety). Semicolons separate summands and commas separate entries within one multidegree. You can also enter taut_quot(X, 2) for a quotient bundle. Use quot(E,F) or Quot(E,F) for a quotient of two bundle expressions; the second argument must be a subbundle of the first. The compact aliases O(1), S(2), and Q(2) are also accepted and are bound to the current variety; use the number of entries required by the kept roots (for example O(1,0) on a two-generator flag). The GUI uses compact text: Python API notation such as [[3]] is not valid in this field.
  • Curve class β: enter one nonnegative integer per kept root, in the order shown in Kept simple roots. A zero-padded vector with one entry per ambient root is also accepted; entries at removed roots must be zero.
  • Insertions: pt, id, or reduced minimal Weyl words separated by |. Copy words printed by Space Info, or click Add beside a basis word.

Evaluate y is optional and applies to quantum matrices only. Variables use ambient node labels (y1, y3, ...), so a variety with kept roots 1,3 uses y1 and y3. Leave it blank for symbolic Novikov variables, or enter assignments such as y1=1,y3=1.

docs.title: Beginner path: direct flags and products
docs.text: For an untwisted direct flag, leave K blank. For example, A2 with kept roots 1 is P²; choose Describe this space first, then choose Compute quantum matrix. A product flag can be entered in the same form: A1xA1, kept roots 1,2, and blank K describes (P¹)².

docs.title: Advanced path: bundle expressions and GW insertions
docs.text:
After Space Info displays the Schubert basis, use its Add controls to build a valid insertion list. This avoids having to know reduced Weyl words in advance. For a homogeneous bundle, first describe the space with the bundle expression, then run the desired matrix or invariant action. taut_quot(X, 2) is directly convex on A4, kept roots 2. The parser also accepts taut_sub(X, 2), but its negative splitting degrees make the supported convex Euler-twisted computation reject that direct input; use dual(taut_sub(X, 2)) for the convex dual bundle.

Goal Algebra Kept roots K β / insertions P² matrix A2 1 (blank) matrix action evaluated P² matrix A2 1 (blank) matrix action with Evaluate y: y1=2 product flag info A1xA1 1,2 (blank) info action 27 lines on a cubic surface A3 1 3 β 1 (or 1,0,0), insertions blank 2875 lines on a quintic A4 1 5 β 1 (or 1,0,0,0), insertions blank Gr(2,4) invariant A3 2 (blank) β 1 (or 0,1,0); 2 1 3 2|1 2|3 2 quotient bundle A4 2 taut_quot(X, 2) describe or matrix action convex dual subbundle A4 2 dual(taut_sub(X, 2)) describe action

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
Space Info reports dimension, Fano index, first Chern class, number of curve classes, and the Schubert basis. Use the Add buttons to build insertion lists.

Quantum matrix reports the matrix, grading, characteristic polynomial, and numerical eigenvalues only when all Novikov variables are specialized to one. A custom Evaluate y value is reported separately and does not claim to be the y=1 spectrum.

GW invariant reports the insertion list, the canonical ambient form of β, and the computed number. The degree-zero API path is a classical cup-integral shortcut, including two-point pairings; it is not the definition of an unstable degree-zero GW invariant.

The toolbar above Results keeps the interface reproducible: Copy input JSON copies the current algebra, kept roots, bundle, β, insertions, and options; Download result JSON saves those inputs together with the exact returned matrix, invariant, or space description.

docs.title: Mathematical scope and conventions
docs.text:
The localization formulas use virtual localization on decorated trees. For a complete intersection, the software requires curvewise convexity and computes the Euler-twisted ambient invariant. For the standard geometric interpretation, assume global generation and a regular section with a smooth zero locus of the expected codimension.

The quantum matrix is the flag-ambient operator described above. It is the full small quantum-cohomology operator only when the relevant homology and ambient-completeness hypotheses hold. For complete intersections, the published matrix is an ambient block.

Automatic curve enumeration needs strictly positive first-Chern pairings on the enumerated curve generators. Mixed zero/positive or negative pairings require an explicit Python betas list, unless a supported constructor supplies effective generators with a positive bound. The all-zero Chern class gives a zero multiplication operator. The reported index uses the specified ambient lattice; see the API conventions.

docs.title: Advanced bundle syntax
docs.text: Supported constructors include O(a,...), S(node), Q(node), taut_quot(X, k), taut_sub(X, k), dual(...), osum(...), tensor(...), sym(...), wedge(...), and quot(E,F) (also Quot(E,F)). The compact aliases omit X; the explicit Python spellings remain available. Use the GUI help text for compact line-bundle rows. Nested lists such as [[3]] belong to the Python API only.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Check that kept roots are valid, distinct node numbers in the algebra and in the intended order.
  • β is normally entered in kept-root order; a full ambient vector is accepted only when all removed-root entries are zero.
  • Insertion words must contain integers separated by spaces; separate multiple insertions with |.
  • A catalog entry marked Catalog only has no supported input or computed matrix provided on this site.
  • If a computation is slow, lower the worker count or start with a preset of lower degree.
  • Catalog matrices are rendered by MathJax. If you copy one into a LaTeX document, load amsmath and raise the column limit for the wider matrices:
\usepackage{amsmath}
\setcounter{MaxMatrixCols}{50}

From the repository root, python3 scripts/validate_catalog_tex.py compiles all catalog display blocks in a temporary document.

docs.title: Python and CLI
docs.text:
from gwflags import FlagVariety
X = FlagVariety('A3', [1])
print(X.gw([], beta=(1,), K=[[3]]))       # 27 (kept-root basis)
print(X.gw([], beta=(1, 0, 0), K=[[3]]))  # same, zero-padded form

For the CLI, put bundle options before the subcommand:

python3 -m gwflags.cli A3 --keep 1 -K 3 sqm

docs.title: Bundle combinations: detailed walkthroughs
docs.text: All bundle examples below use the same ambient variety: X = Gr(2,5), entered as algebra A4 with kept roots 2. Begin with Describe this space to confirm the basis and dimension. Then enter one of the following expressions in Bundle K and choose Compute quantum matrix or Describe this space.

docs.title: 1. Quotient bundle
docs.text:
GUI input (both spellings are accepted):

taut_quot(X, 2)
Q(2)

This is the rank-3 tautological quotient bundle. Leave Evaluate y blank for symbolic variables, or use y2=1 for specialization (the kept node is 2). The result summary records the submitted bundle expression, and the matrix is computed using the quotient-bundle twist.

Equivalent Python:

from gwflags import FlagVariety
from gwflags.bundles import taut_quot

X = FlagVariety('A4', [2])
Q = taut_quot(X, 2)
M, grading, basis = X.small_quantum_multiplication(K=Q)

docs.title: 2. Quotient of two bundle expressions
docs.text:
Use quot(E,F) (or the capitalized spelling Quot(E,F)) when F is a subbundle of E:

quot(osum(S(2),Q(2)), S(2))

Here E = S(2) ⊕ Q(2) is a direct sum, and quotienting by its first summand gives the rank-3 bundle Q(2). The tautological exact sequence 0 → S(2) → O⁵ → Q(2) → 0 gives the same class in K-theory as O⁵, but does not identify this direct sum with a trivial vector bundle. The software checks the fiber-weight multisets with multiplicity at every fixed point (equivalent type-A characters are compared after removing the torus-trivial trace direction). Different varieties or a missing weight produce a clear validation error.

Weight containment is a necessary consistency check; it does not construct a subbundle embedding or determine arbitrary extension data. The caller must supply a genuine quotient with supported invariant-curve restrictions.

Equivalent Python:

from gwflags.bundles import osum, quot, taut_sub, taut_quot
E = osum(taut_sub(X, 2), taut_quot(X, 2))
F = taut_sub(X, 2)
K = quot(E, F)
assert K.rank == 3

docs.title: 3. Dual of the tautological subbundle
docs.text:
The subbundle itself is generally not convex for the twisted genus-0 theory. Use its dual instead:

dual(S(2))

The explicit equivalent dual(taut_sub(X, 2)) is also accepted.

Equivalent Python:

from gwflags.bundles import taut_sub, dual
K = dual(taut_sub(X, 2))
M, grading, basis = X.small_quantum_multiplication(K=K)

The GUI accepts the expression, while a direct taut_sub(X, 2) computation may be rejected when its curve splitting degrees are negative.

docs.title: 4. Direct sum of bundles
docs.text:
Use osum to combine summands. This example combines the rank-3 quotient with a line bundle O(1) on this Picard-rank-one Grassmannian:

osum(Q(2), O(1))

The explicit equivalent osum(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1)) is also accepted.

On Gr(2,5) there is one kept node, so O(X, 1) takes one degree. A two-entry constructor such as O(X, 1, 1) belongs on a two-generator product (for example A2xA2, kept roots 1,3). In the compact GUI syntax, separate summands are written as rows such as 1;2.

Python:

from gwflags.bundles import O, osum, taut_quot
K = osum(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1))
print(K.rank)  # 4

docs.title: 5. Tensor product
docs.text:
tensor forms all pairwise sums of fiber weights:

tensor(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1))

Python:

from gwflags.bundles import O, tensor, taut_quot
K = tensor(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1))
print(K.rank)  # 3

docs.title: 6. Symmetric and exterior powers
docs.text:
These constructors derive new bundles from a homogeneous bundle:

sym(2, taut_quot(X, 2))
wedge(2, taut_quot(X, 2))

The first has rank 6 and the second rank 3. In Python:

from gwflags.bundles import taut_quot, sym, wedge
Q = taut_quot(X, 2)
print(sym(2, Q).rank)    # 6
print(wedge(2, Q).rank)  # 3

docs.title: Combining several operations
docs.text:
Expressions can be nested, provided every component is built on the same X:

osum(
  tensor(Q(2), O(1)),
  wedge(2, dual(S(2)))
)

For long expressions, Python is easier to read and debug. The GUI parser only allows the documented constructors and rejects arbitrary Python code.

docs.title: What to check before computing
docs.text:
1. Confirm that every component uses the same algebra and kept nodes.
  2. Use Describe this space first; it reports the resulting bundle rank.
  3. Ensure the combined bundle is curvewise convex for the requested twisted computation. A non-convex bundle is reported as an error rather than being silently accepted.
  4. Start with symbolic y variables. Specialize with Evaluate y only after the symbolic matrix has been assembled.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Choose the path that matches your background. You do not need SageMath to use the browser interface or the core Python API.

docs.text:
1. Install Python 3.9 or newer (Python 3.10+ is recommended) from python.org. On Windows, select Add Python to PATH.

docs.title: Comfortable with Python
docs.text:
From a checkout, activate your existing environment and run python -m pip install -e .. Then use the GUI, CLI, or import FlagVariety in a script. Run a quick smoke test:

python -c "from gwflags import FlagVariety; print(FlagVariety('A2',[1]).dimension)"

To run the tests, install the optional test dependency first:

python -m pip install -e ".[test]"

Then run the full tests with:

python -m pytest tests/ -q

docs.title: SageMath users
docs.text: SageMath is optional. If it is installed, gwflags can use it for symbolic work; the plain Python installation above remains the supported baseline. On Windows, use WSL for SageMath and follow the Linux commands there.

docs.title: Defining Flag Varieties \(G/P\) in Our Software
docs.text: This guide explains how to construct complex flag varieties \(G/P\) using our software by specifying a Cartan Type (to define the complex semisimple Lie group \(G\)) and Keep Nodes (to define the parabolic subgroup \(P\)).

docs.title: 1. The Lie-Theoretic Setup
docs.text:
Let \(G\) be a complex semisimple Lie group. We use its simply connected form to label line bundles by fundamental weights: \(SL(n)\), \(Spin(n)\), or \(Sp(2n)\) in the classical cases. The orthogonal descriptions below can also be written with \(SO(n)\), which has the same flag varieties. Its Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g}\) is classified by a Cartan Type and a Dynkin diagram; simple roots are indexed by Bourbaki node numbers.

A standard parabolic subgroup \(P \subset G\) is determined by a subset of the simple roots. In our software, you specify \(P\) by providing the Keep Nodes (using the --keep argument in the CLI or "Keep Nodes" in the GUI). Geometrically, specifying a node \(k\) in "Keep Nodes" corresponds to crossing out that node \(k\) from the Dynkin diagram. This omits the \(k\)-th simple root from the Levi factor of \(P\) (which is equivalent to keeping the \(k\)-th fundamental weight). Thus, if you specify a single node \(k\) in Keep Nodes, node \(k\) is crossed out, making \(P\) a maximal parabolic subgroup, and \(G/P\) is a generalized Grassmannian.

docs.title: 2. Dictionary of Standard Geometric Spaces
docs.text: Below is the explicit mapping from classical geometric spaces to their corresponding (Cartan Type, Keep Nodes) inputs.

docs.title: Projective Spaces \(\mathbb{P}^n\)
docs.text: The complex projective space \(\mathbb{P}^n\) is the space of 1-dimensional subspaces in \(\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\). - Group: \(G = SL(n+1)\) - Cartan Type: $A_n$ - Keep Nodes: 1 (or n for the dual projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{n\ast}\)) - Example: To construct \(\mathbb{P}^4\), use Algebra = A4, Keep Nodes = 1.

docs.title: Grassmannians \(Gr(k, n)\)
docs.text: The Grassmannian \(Gr(k, n)\) is the space of \(k\)-dimensional subspaces in \(\mathbb{C}^n\). - Group: \(G = SL(n)\) - Cartan Type: $A_{n-1}$ - Keep Nodes: k - Example: To construct \(Gr(2, 5)\), use Algebra = A4, Keep Nodes = 2.

docs.title: Lagrangian Grassmannians \(LG(n, 2n)\)
docs.text: The Lagrangian Grassmannian \(LG(n, 2n)\) parameterizes \(n\)-dimensional isotropic subspaces of a \(2n\)-dimensional symplectic vector space. - Group: \(G = Sp(2n)\) - Cartan Type: $C_n$ - Keep Nodes: n - Example: To construct \(LG(3, 6)\), use Algebra = C3, Keep Nodes = 3.

docs.title: Odd Orthogonal Grassmannians \(OG(n, 2n+1)\)
docs.text: This space parameterizes \(n\)-dimensional isotropic subspaces of a \((2n+1)\)-dimensional orthogonal vector space. - Group: \(G = SO(2n+1)\) - Cartan Type: $B_n$ - Keep Nodes: n - Example: To construct \(OG(3, 7)\), use Algebra = B3, Keep Nodes = 3.

docs.title: Even Orthogonal Grassmannians \(OG(n, 2n)\) (Spinor Varieties)
docs.text: This space has two connected components, each parameterizing one family of \(n\)-dimensional isotropic subspaces in a \(2n\)-dimensional orthogonal vector space. - Group: \(G = SO(2n)\) - Cartan Type: D_n - Keep Nodes: n (or n-1 for the other connected component) - Example: To construct \(OG(4, 8)\), use Algebra = D4, Keep Nodes = 4.

docs.title: 3. References
docs.text:
On the maximal orthogonal Grassmannians above, O(1) denotes the primitive spinor generator. The Plücker determinant line bundle is O(2). This matters when translating section degrees into Bundle K; the two conventions must not be interchanged.

For rigorous foundations of Lie algebras, root systems, Dynkin diagrams, and the construction of homogeneous spaces, please refer to the following standard texts:

  1. Fulton, W., & Harris, J. (1991). Representation Theory: A First Course. Springer.
  2. Humphreys, J. E. (1972). Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory. Springer.

docs.title: Methods and conventions
docs.text: gwflags computes genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariants and small quantum multiplication by the first Chern class. For a flag variety \(F=G/P\), it uses Schubert classes. For a complete intersection \(Y\subset F\), the returned matrix describes the flag-ambient sector: the cohomology classes obtained by restriction from \(F\).

docs.title: Quantum multiplication
docs.text:
Let \(\{\phi_i\}\) be a cohomology basis and \(\{\phi^i\}\) its dual for the Poincaré pairing. The small quantum product is [ \alpha\star\delta =\sum_{\beta,i}q^\beta \langle\alpha,\delta,\phi_i\rangle_{0,3,\beta}\,\phi^i. ] The degree-zero term is the cup product. In a general basis, forming its matrix requires the inverse pairing as well as the three-point invariants. The software specializes to \(\alpha=c_1(TY)\).

Matrix columns are inputs and rows are outputs. The returned grading is diagonal, with entries \(\operatorname{codim}(\phi_i)-\dim(Y)/2\). Catalog matrices use all Novikov variables \(y_i=1\) unless explicitly labelled symbolic. The download preserves both forms and the ordered basis.

docs.title: Virtual localization
docs.text:
The torus action on \(G/P\) induces an action on the moduli space of stable maps. Its genus-zero fixed loci are indexed by decorated trees: vertices map to torus-fixed points and edges cover invariant curves. The software sums their contributions using the virtual-localization formula of Graber and Pandharipande, Localization of virtual classes.

Calculations use exact rational arithmetic. The default implementation evaluates the localization sum at two rational torus points and compares the results; the symbolic path is also available. Agreement is a consistency check, not an independent proof of every formula in the implementation.

docs.title: Complete intersections and the ambient sector
docs.text:
For a bundle \(E\) on \(F\), the supported Euler-twisted calculation requires nonnegative splitting degrees along the relevant invariant curves. A standard geometric interpretation assumes a globally generated bundle and a regular section with smooth zero locus \(Y\). Then [ \dim Y=\dim F-\operatorname{rank}E,\qquad c_1(TY)=\bigl(c_1(TF)-c_1(E)\bigr)|_Y. ]

The software forms the classical twisted pairing [ g_{ij}=\int_F\sigma_i\sigma_j e(E) ] and selects a nondegenerate submatrix to obtain its ambient basis. Primitive cohomology is not supplied by this reduction. Identifying the output with the full quantum-cohomology operator requires the corresponding homology and ambient-completeness hypotheses.

Fixed-point weights alone do not determine the curve restrictions of an arbitrary non-split bundle. Quotient constructions must come from a genuine geometric quotient with supported restriction data; weight containment is a consistency check rather than a proof of a bundle embedding.

docs.title: Curve degrees and index
docs.text:
For positive degree and \(n\) primary insertions, the dimension axiom is [ \sum_i\operatorname{codim}(\alpha_i) =\dim Y+\langle c_1(TY),\beta\rangle+n-3. ] For multiplication by \(c_1\), it bounds contributing degrees by \(\langle c_1(TY),\beta\rangle\leq\dim Y+1\). This gives a finite automatic list when every enumerated curve generator has positive Chern pairing. A zero direction in an otherwise nonzero Chern vector is not bounded by this inequality. Such cases, and negative pairings, require explicit curve lists unless a supported constructor supplies effective generators with a positive bound. If the entire Chern class vanishes, its multiplication operator is zero.

The catalog’s Ambient Index is the gcd of the Chern pairings in the specified ambient curve lattice (or a constructor’s effective generators). It agrees with the geometric Fano index when the relevant integral-lattice identification holds. A smooth conic illustrates the distinction: it is \(\mathbb P^1\), with geometric index 2, while its ambient Chern gcd in \(\mathbb P^2\) is 1. This gcd does not define a geometric Fano index for a point. The software and JSON retain the field name fano_index.

The Python API specifies kept-root coordinates, basis indices and the degree-zero classical-pairing shortcut. The user guide gives copyable inputs.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The test suite checks known enumerative values, including the line through two points of \(\mathbb P^2\), 27 lines on a cubic surface and 2875 lines on a quintic threefold. Catalog checks compare saved matrices with their inputs, bases, gradings, degree constraints and characteristic polynomials. Displayed spectra are checked numerically, while projective Hodge diamonds are checked by exact Riemann–Roch and Lefschetz calculations.

These checks are reproducible in the repository:

python -m pip install -r requirements-test.txt
python -m pytest tests/ -q
python scripts/validate_localization_results.py
python scripts/validate_catalog_math.py

Checking saved outputs does not rerun all localization sums or prove every geometric realization in the reference catalog. To reproduce a matrix, use its input with the software; Catalog only entries have no supported computed matrix.

docs.title: Download matrices and inputs
docs.text:
This download lets you reuse the matrices displayed in the catalog in Python, SageMath or other software, or repeat the computations from their original inputs. It includes the basis order and grading needed to interpret each matrix.

You can read the examples directly in the catalog; the download is optional. Exact means that fractions and symbolic expressions are preserved instead of rounded decimal approximations.

The fano_index field uses the software’s ambient Chern-lattice convention; it need not be the intrinsic Fano index of a low-dimensional section. For example, a conic is P1 with geometric index 2 even when the ambient gcd is 1. See catalog conventions.

This collection contains 131 completed exact localization computations, including 32 threefold realizations. Different realizations are listed separately even when the resulting varieties are isomorphic.

Download the complete JSON dataset

Each record contains the executable algebra/kept-root/bundle input, the full automatically supported curve list in ambient coordinates, the symbolic \(c_1(TY)\) multiplication matrix, its specialization at all \(y_i=1\), the ordered Schubert basis, and the grading. Rational numbers are stored as exact strings. The matrix acts on the returned ambient sector, with columns as inputs and rows as outputs.

These are the same results displayed in the catalog. See Methods and conventions for their mathematical scope.

docs.title: Use a saved result
docs.text:
import json
from pathlib import Path

data = json.loads(Path("localization-results.json").read_text())
example = next(r for r in data["examples"] if r["id"] == "e1322438fd01")
print(example["input"])
print(example["matrix_symbolic"])
print(example["basis_words"])

To recompute a record, construct FlagVariety with its algebra and kept roots, parse its bundle using the documented input syntax, and call small_quantum_multiplication(K) without restricting the automatic curve list.

docs.title: Grassmannians
docs.text:
Index convention: the displayed Ambient Index is the software's ambient Chern gcd. A smooth conic has geometric index 2 even when this field is 1; the zero-dimensional linear section is a point, for which this gcd does not define a geometric Fano index. See the catalog conventions.

This section contains complete intersections inside this geometric family, systematically organized by dimension and ambient index.

For the kept-root beta convention and copyable browser/CLI syntax, see How to Use.

docs.title: Reproduce an entry in the software
docs.text: For a Grassmannian Gr(k,n), run A(n-1) with Kept simple roots k. Each displayed / O(d) is one row in Bundle K: enter d, or enter d1;d2;... for several summands. For example, Gr(2,6) / O(1)+O(2) is A5, kept roots 2, and Bundle K 1;2 (or [[1],[2]] in Python). The card's dimension is k(n-k) minus the number of rows, and its ambient index is n - sum(d). This convention also covers the dual presentation Gr(n-k,n) shown in the catalog.

docs.title: Projective Spaces
docs.text:
Index convention: the displayed Ambient Index is the software's ambient Chern gcd. In particular, P2 / O(2) has displayed index 1 but is a smooth conic, hence P1, with geometric Fano index 2. See the catalog conventions.

This section contains complete intersections inside this geometric family, systematically organized by dimension and ambient index.

For the kept-root beta convention and copyable browser/CLI syntax, see How to Use.

docs.title: Reproduce an entry in the software
docs.text: Every card below is a complete intersection in projective space. For the ambient space $P^n$, run A(n) with Kept simple roots 1. Each displayed summand / O(d) is one row in Bundle K: enter d for one summand, or d1;d2;... for several summands. For example, the card P8 / O(2)+O(3) is reproduced with A8, kept roots 1, and Bundle K 2;3 (or [[2],[3]] in Python). The card's dimension is n minus the number of rows, and its ambient index is n+1 - sum(d); these provide quick checks that the input matches the card.
